messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Airline Pilot
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
John, a 63-year-old airline pilot of Oceania descent, has been haunted by his combat experiences for years. During a mission in Afghanistan, he was involved in an intense firefight while on a helicopter reconnaissance mission at dusk. The tactile memory of the rough sand and the constant whirring noise of the helicopters' rotors have become potent triggers for John. Every time he feels a similar texture or hears a sound reminiscent of those moments, he is instantly transported back to that terrifying experience. John’s night vigilance is particularly pronounced; the darkness seems to amplify his sense of vulnerability. Each evening, as twilight begins to fall, he finds it increasingly difficult to feel safe. The same time of day when the traumatic event occurred intensifies his anxiety, making him hyper-aware and on edge. Even at home with his wife, he scans the room continuously for exits and remains vigilant about sudden movements by others, always ready to react defensively. His memories of that fateful mission are fragmented and feel alien to him. Despite being a key participant in those events, John often struggles to integrate these memories into his sense of self. When triggered, these memories return with a terrifying force, reenacting the intense fear he felt at the time. The sudden recall is often precipitated by an auditory cue or a particular texture, leaving him feeling disoriented and overwhelmed. John’s negative appraisals have significantly impacted his outlook on life and himself. He harbors deep-seated beliefs that there is something fundamentally wrong with him as a person. This self-perception has eroded much of the joy he once found in life. What was once filled with happiness now feels perpetually dark and miserable. The constant vigilance and fear have made it difficult for John to engage fully with his work or his relationships, including that with his wife. Over time, these avoidance behaviors have taken a toll on both his professional and personal life. He has become increasingly isolated at home, avoiding social gatherings and family outings where the risk of being exposed to triggers is high. His job as an airline pilot requires him to be in constant proximity to aircraft sounds, making each day a potential trigger for his symptoms. John’s colleagues have noticed changes in his demeanor; he appears more distant and preoccupied. John has also begun to avoid certain aspects of his daily routine. For instance, he no longer walks the familiar paths near his home that are lined with sand-like textures reminiscent of the desert sands where his traumatic experiences took place. This avoidance has gradually isolated him from activities he once enjoyed, leaving him feeling more disconnected from both his work and personal life. The cumulative impact of these symptoms finally pushed John to seek help after a particularly distressing episode at work. During a routine flight, the sound of another helicopter passing overhead triggered a full relapse of his traumatic memories. He experienced such intense fear that he was unable to focus on flying safely for several minutes, leading to a near-miss incident that could have had catastrophic consequences. This close call was a wake-up call for John. He realized that his condition is not only affecting him but also putting others at risk. What frightens him most is the thought of losing control again in such critical situations and endangering lives. At the same time, he is hopeful that with professional help, he can regain some measure of peace and stability. John’s journey to seek help reflects a deep-seated fear of being permanently damaged by his experiences but also a glimmer of hope for recovery. He hopes to reclaim parts of his life that have been lost to the constant vigilance and terror that now dominate his existence.
